analysis.one_liner: Requires meatpackers to publicly report cattle contracts and buy a minimum share of cattle in open cash markets.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, introduced by a Republican with Democratic support, sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing, vote, or floor action until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force big cattle slaughterers ("packers") to file their standard cattle purchase contracts into a public library, so ranchers can see what terms are actually being offered. It would also require USDA to set regional minimums on how much cattle packers must buy through open, negotiated cash deals — the trades that set market prices — and to publicly report slaughter schedules 14 days ahead. The goal is more visible price-setting in a market where a handful of packers buy most cattle through private formula deals.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and feeders, who sell to a handful of dominant meatpacking companies. The public contract library would let them see the actual contract terms available, the reporting of forward slaughter schedules would show where cattle are needed, and mandated minimums of open cash trading would strengthen the price discovery that determines what ranchers are paid. Consumers who buy beef benefit indirectly from a more transparent price-setting process.

how_it_helps.text: USDA must create and maintain a publicly available library of the types of contracts packers offer to, and open to, producers for buying fed cattle, including premium and discount schedules [S2][S3].

USDA must set regional mandatory minimums on the number and share of cattle packers must buy through negotiated (cash) or negotiated grid purchases, with the methods published and subject to public comment, to enhance price discovery and transparency [S2][S3].

Packers must report each day, by 10 a.m., the number of cattle scheduled for delivery for slaughter over the next 14 days, and the bill bars USDA from withholding the market information it collects from the public [S3].
The bill makes it unlawful for a packer to willfully refuse to provide the required information [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large meatpacking companies (packers) that buy most cattle. They bear new reporting and filing duties, and the regional mandatory minimums would force a share of their cattle purchases out of private formula and forward contracts into open negotiated markets, where competing bids can drive prices up. Consumer beef prices could rise modestly if packers pass on costs.

drawbacks.text: Packers and some industry groups argue that government-mandated minimums on cash purchases can reduce packing flexibility and efficiency, and that added costs could end up in consumer beef prices [S3].

The contract library is funded only "subject to the availability of appropriations," so Congress would still have to fund it, and the mandatory minimums would not take effect until two years after enactment with further cost-benefit review three years after that, slowing any benefit [S3].

The initial regional minimums are set no lower than the recent three-year average of negotiated purchases, so in regions where open-cash trading has already collapsed the floor could lock in a very thin cash market rather than rebuild it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ranchers in a market where four packers buy the vast majority of cattle, the transparency and price-discovery provisions address a real, documented power imbalance, and the costs fall mainly on the packers it targets. The honest caveats are design ones: the minimums could be set too low to matter, the mandate timeline is slow, and consumers may absorb some cost. On balance the bill's benefits for market transparency outweigh its drawbacks, though it is not a fix for packer concentration itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced March 2, 2021 by Sen. Fischer with three cosponsors (one Democrat, two Republicans), it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1][S3][S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee markup, no discharge petition, and no floor vote through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies that dominate cattle buying came out ahead: no public contract library, no required publication of slaughter schedules, and no mandatory minimums of open cash-market purchases ever took effect. Ranchers are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed the cattle contract library and regional price-discovery minimums.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole Democratic cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: 2 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, Braun of Indiana)

against.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: The committee referred to never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's record shows no action after its referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Major beef packers
against.role: Four companies processing most U.S. cattle
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandates requiring them to buy minimum shares of cattle in open cash markets, the provision that would most change how they buy cattle.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with three cosponsors split 3 Republican and 1 Democrat; no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so no vote breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would require packers to file their cattle contracts into a public library, report 14-day slaughter schedules daily, and buy a minimum share of cattle through open negotiated markets — all measures that weaken their control over price setting. The industry's interest in blocking this runs against the ranchers and consumers the transparency serves.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and feedlot operators
industries.note: Ranchers would gain visibility into real contract terms and a stronger cash market for price discovery, which sets what they are paid for cattle. They are the bill's intended beneficiaries.
